explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Isaiah says, "Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse…" (Isaiah 11:1). Everybody figures a stump is finished, but something green comes up out of it anyway. I know a little about being written off, and I like this kind of surprise.

I get why a thornbush came to mind, since stumps don't exactly look friendly. But Isaiah says, "Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse…" (Isaiah 11:1). A shoot is a young green sprout, and it's the opposite of a prickly mess. The stump belongs to Jesse, King David's father (Ruth 4:22).

A cedar would be a big dramatic answer, and I respect the ambition. Isaiah goes smaller, though: "Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse…" (Isaiah 11:1). A shoot is a tiny new sprout, not a full-grown tree. It starts small, and I think that's the whole charm.

I see why you'd worry, since stumps don't have the best reputation. But Isaiah says the opposite. "…a Branch from his roots will bear fruit." (Isaiah 11:1). Nothing withers here, baker. This Branch bears fruit.

That's right. Isaiah says, "…a Branch from his roots will bear fruit." (Isaiah 11:1). Bearing fruit is the opposite of withering. A stump that was supposed to be done is about to produce, and I'm rooting for that stump.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "And He will delight in the fear of the LORD." (Isaiah 11:3). Delight means he's not dragging his feet about it. He enjoys it, and honestly, I wish I enjoyed Monday mornings that much.

I can see how that slipped in, but the text goes the other way. Isaiah says, "And He will delight in the fear of the LORD." (Isaiah 11:3). There's no doubt anywhere in that verse. The word the text uses is delight.

Hiding is a very human instinct, I'll admit. I spent years stuck in the back of a junk drawer, so I'm not judging. But Isaiah says, "And He will delight in the fear of the LORD." (Isaiah 11:3). Hiding isn't the word in the verse. Delight is.

That sounds sensible, because most of us judge by what we see and hear. But Isaiah says, "He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear…" (Isaiah 11:3). So the Branch doesn't go by appearances or by hearsay. The statement was the opposite of what the text says.

Right. Isaiah says, "He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear…" (Isaiah 11:3). Not by what He sees, and not by what He hears. The text says what He will do instead in the next verse.

That's it. Isaiah says, "…with righteousness He will judge the poor…" (Isaiah 11:4). The poor are the ones He judges with righteousness. The next line adds that He will decide with equity "…for the lowly of the earth."

The powerful are who most of us expect a judge to be busy with. But Isaiah says, "…with righteousness He will judge the poor…" (Isaiah 11:4). The poor are named here, and the powerful aren't. This Branch is paying attention to the ones the world overlooks.

Priests would be a very official guess, and I admire the formality. But Isaiah says, "…with righteousness He will judge the poor…" (Isaiah 11:4). The next line adds that He will decide with equity "…for the lowly of the earth." The text names the poor and the lowly.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth…" (Isaiah 11:4). The rod is of His mouth. I bet that's a picture of how much His words weigh.

explanations.answer: An iron rod in His hand
explanations.explanation: An iron rod is a very reasonable guess for a rod. But Isaiah says, "He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth…" (Isaiah 11:4). The text says the rod of His mouth, not an iron rod. That's a different picture from what you picked.

Swords and armies are the usual way kings do things. Isaiah says something different: "He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth…" (Isaiah 11:4). No army is mentioned in that verse. It's all in His mouth.

Yes. Isaiah says, "Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist." (Isaiah 11:5). So He wears both righteousness and faithfulness. I can only dream of an outfit that good, and my apron has flour stains on it.

I can see wondering if only one made the list. But Isaiah says, "Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist." (Isaiah 11:5). Righteousness is the belt and faithfulness is the sash, so He wears both. That makes this statement true.

A wolf hunting a lamb is how we'd normally expect it to go. But Isaiah says, "The wolf will live with the lamb…" (Isaiah 11:6). In this picture, the wolf lives with the lamb. That's the whole shock of it.
Right. Isaiah says, "The wolf will live with the lamb…" (Isaiah 11:6). A wolf and a lamb sharing a home is not the kind of roommate situation you see every day. Hunting isn't in the picture at all.

That's it. Isaiah says, "…and a little child will lead them." (Isaiah 11:6). The leader is a little child, in a verse full of leopards and young lions. I'd follow that child anywhere, baker, but I'd be hanging back a few steps.

A shepherd would be a sensible leader for a herd, I'll give you that. But Isaiah says, "…and a little child will lead them." (Isaiah 11:6). The one in front is a little child, not a grown-up. That's part of what makes the picture so surprising.
A mighty hunter would be a bold pick in a verse with a young lion in it. Isaiah says, "…and a little child will lead them." (Isaiah 11:6). The leader is a little child, not a hunter.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "…and the lion will eat straw like the ox." (Isaiah 11:7). A lion eating straw. I don't think any lion has put that on a menu yet.

I understand the doubt, since lions and straw don't usually go together. But Isaiah says, "…and the lion will eat straw like the ox." (Isaiah 11:7). That's exactly what he says, so this one is true. It's part of what makes the picture so wild.
That's the one. Isaiah says, "They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain…" (Isaiah 11:9). The verse says all My holy mountain, not just one slope of it.

Growing old or weary sounds like a nice thing to be free of, and I'd sign up. But it's not in the verse. Isaiah says, "They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain…" (Isaiah 11:9). Harming and destroying are what's gone.

Buying and selling is a reasonable thing to think of, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says, "They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain…" (Isaiah 11:9). Harming and destroying are what won't happen.

That's the first blank, baker. Isaiah says the earth "…will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." (Isaiah 11:9). Knowledge fills the earth the way water fills the sea. There's no dry spot.

Yes, that's the second blank. Isaiah says the earth "…will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." (Isaiah 11:9). It's knowledge of the LORD that fills the earth. The sea is the comparison for how full that knowledge will be.

Anger is a word that fits the mood of a lot of days, I admit. But Isaiah says the earth "…will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." (Isaiah 11:9). Anger isn't in the verse. Knowledge of the LORD is what fills the earth.

Kings are an easy word to grab, since this passage has a lot of royal talk. But the verse says the earth "…will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." (Isaiah 11:9). Kings don't fill the earth here. Knowledge does.

Silver would be nice for my cookie box budget. But Isaiah says the earth "…will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water." (Isaiah 11:9). What fills it is knowledge, not silver.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "The nations will seek Him…" (Isaiah 11:10). The banner isn't just for one group. It's for the peoples, and the nations come looking.

Angels are a nice thought. I've met the angel who called me out of that drawer, so I know they take the Lord's business seriously. But Isaiah says, "The nations will seek Him…" (Isaiah 11:10). The ones doing the seeking are the nations.

I see why you'd guess the wicked, since they were mentioned earlier in the passage. But Isaiah says, "The nations will seek Him…" (Isaiah 11:10). The nations are the ones seeking. The wicked aren't named in this verse.

explanations.answer: The four corners of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Isaiah says, "He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth." (Isaiah 11:12). That's about as far apart as people can get. And He collects them anyway.

explanations.answer: The far side of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The far side of the Jordan is a real place, but it's not what the verse says. Isaiah says, "He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth." (Isaiah 11:12). That's a much bigger circle than one river.

explanations.answer: The plains of Moab near Jericho
explanations.explanation: Moab and Jericho are real places, and I like that you went specific. But Isaiah says, "He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth." (Isaiah 11:12). The four corners of the earth is the whole map. That's quite a bit bigger than one plain.

Envy can be stubborn, I'll grant you that. But Isaiah says, "Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor will Judah harass Ephraim." (Isaiah 11:13). The envy ends, and so does the harassing. Both sides get to put the grudge down.
Right. Isaiah says, "Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor will Judah harass Ephraim." (Isaiah 11:13). The envy is gone, and the harassing is gone too. Peace between those two is quite a change.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says the LORD "…will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals." (Isaiah 11:15). Crossing with dry sandals means nobody gets wet feet. I'm a big fan of dry feet, especially around the bakery.

Wet sandals would be the sensible guess for a river. But Isaiah says the LORD "…will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals." (Isaiah 11:15). So this one is true. The crossing is dry.

explanations.answer: When Israel came up from Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's it. Isaiah says, "There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt." (Isaiah 11:16). It points back to that earlier journey out of Egypt. A highway will be there for them again.

explanations.answer: When Abram set out from Ur
explanations.explanation: Abram, the man God later named Abraham (Genesis 17:5), did make a famous journey from Ur (Genesis 11:31). But Isaiah doesn't compare the highway to that trip. He says it will be "…as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt." (Isaiah 11:16). The comparison is to the journey out of Egypt.

Jacob, Isaac's son, did travel to Haran (Genesis 28:10). Isaiah doesn't use that trip, though. He says the highway will be "…as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt." (Isaiah 11:16). The comparison is the journey out of Egypt.

Yes, baker. The speaker says, "Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me." (Isaiah 12:1). The anger has turned away, and comfort has come. I can hear the relief in that line.

I can see why that might come to mind after reading about judgment earlier. But the speaker says, "Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me." (Isaiah 12:1). The anger isn't growing. It has turned away.

A lot of us brace for the other shoe to drop, I know I do. But the speaker says, "Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me." (Isaiah 12:1). The words say it has turned away. Nothing in the verse mentions it returning.
That's right. The speaker says, "…Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me." (Isaiah 12:1). Comfort is named right there. I think the speaker is grateful for it, and I'd be too.
I see why the earlier anger might make you hesitate. But the speaker says, "…Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me." (Isaiah 12:1). The comfort is stated plainly, so this one is true.

That's it, baker. The speaker says, "Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid." (Isaiah 12:2). Trusting and not being afraid goes together right after that line. I know a little about the dark, and I like this one.

Staying quiet is something I know a lot about, thanks to my years in the back of a junk drawer. But that's not what the speaker says. It's "Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid." (Isaiah 12:2). Trust is what comes next, and fear is out.
Running to Egypt for help is a different move than the one here. The speaker says, "Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid." (Isaiah 12:2). The speaker looks to God, not to Egypt.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation…" (Isaiah 12:3). They draw the water with joy. I'd say that's the best way to fill a bucket.

I see why tears might fit, since tears and water are close cousins. But Isaiah says, "With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation…" (Isaiah 12:3). The word is joy. It's a glad kind of drawing.
Fear would make for a nervous trip to the well. But Isaiah says, "With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation…" (Isaiah 12:3). Joy is the word, and fear isn't part of this scene.
That's right. The words say, "Make His works known among the peoples…" (Isaiah 12:4). It's not kept inside one group. It goes out to the peoples.

The temple courts are a fair guess for a praise song. But the words say, "Make His works known among the peoples…" (Isaiah 12:4). The reach is among the peoples, which is much wider than one building.
Zion does come up later in this song, so I see the connection. But the words say, "Make His works known among the peoples…" (Isaiah 12:4). The peoples are the ones to hear it, beyond any walls.

Keeping quiet would be the safe thing to do. But the words say, "Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth." (Isaiah 12:5). They don't say keep it quiet. They say let it be known in all the earth.

Right. The words say, "Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth." (Isaiah 12:5). That's the opposite of quiet. The glorious things are meant to be known everywhere.

Far away would be a lonely thing to hear, so I understand the worry. But the last line says, "Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel." (Isaiah 12:6). He's not far off. He is great among them.

That's right. The last line says, "Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel." (Isaiah 12:6). The Holy One of Israel is great right among them. He's close, not far away.
